# Robot Localization

## Luke Wei and Dionysus Lively

Oct 21, 2026  
**Project Purpose**  
Our goal for this project was to create a particle filter that could narrow down the position of a robot in a given map provided it had a good initial guess of the robot’s initial position.  
**Project Overview**  
To continuously localize our robot’s location, we developed base skeleton code to execute the following high-level flow: receive an initial odometry guess for the Neato, create an initial particle cloud, detect minimum movement, generate hundreds of Particle objects that contain locations and random headings in the vicinity of the initial guess, compare lidar data from the Neato to the generated particles and headings using ray tracing and a pre-set map, and resample new particles while injecting uniformly distributed noise. Once new particles are resampled, our main loop repeats the steps following the initial guess; if a new odometry guess is published, however, this entire loop executes before continuously running to the movement-resampling sub-loop.

**Initializing the Particle Filter**  
We used skeleton code for a central ParticleFilter class through which our entire particle filter runs. When a particle filter object is initialized, we hardcode all parameters and non-topic variables used in methods and external functions including: the names of all frames—odometry, base-link, and world or map—the lidar scan topic of the real or simulated Neato to be received, the number of particles to use, and the movement thresholds for running the Neato. We decided to use 600 particles for the final particle filter to compute the accuracy of potential positions in less than 1 second while still converging on a reasonable location; we also used a movement threshold of 2 meters and 30 degrees for calculating new positions to ensure a buffer period of at least 0.4 seconds between position estimates—limited by the max linear and angular velocities that we commanded to the Neato via tele-op. In addition to initializing the particle cloud publisher and the initial pose subscriber in this ParticleFilter initialization function, we also start executing the main loop.

**Initializing the Particle Cloud**  
	Once in the main loop, we first collect an initial guess for the heading of our Neato and then initialize a particle cloud about that same Neato by adding uniformly random noise to both the heading and position of the initial particle. The range for the locations is a 2-meter by 2-meter square centered at the original guess. This 2-meter by 2-meter range covers a breadth of positions in which the Neato is highly likely to exist without diluting the density of particles below 15 particles per Neato or roughly 33cm by 33cm. Statistically, having 15 randomly generated particles per possible Neato location means there is a high likelihood of at least one particle representing a reasonably accurate location with a heading within a 20-degree range of the actual Neato heading. Since our initial cloud generates particles with guesses that are close enough, we are able to reduce the range of noise for resampling as we converge to increasingly accurate positions using the higher weighted particles. This initial particle cloud is used only once to localize the robot after the first time the movement threshold is reached; afterwards, new particle clouds are resampled over a smaller range using calculated particle weights.

**Ray tracing and weighting**  
We decided to assign weights to each particle via ray tracing. What we essentially do is project the actual scan of the Neato onto each particle and see how closely the scans match up. To do this, first we store the data for every 10th index of the Neato’s laser scan. We chose to sample every 10th index in order to lower the compute time. Now that we have the data, we transform that data onto a particle’s location. If the nearest obstacle is within a certain threshold of the tip of a beam, we consider the beam as hitting an obstacle. If it isn’t within that threshold, we “march” the beam forward by the distance of the nearest obstacle and rerun the process until the beam registers a hit. Beams that go off of the map are discarded. Then we take the list of lengths of the valid beams and subtract the lengths of real beams from the lengths of the projected beams to get an error for each beam. To weight the beams, we use a Gaussian distribution.

**Particle Resampling**  
Once the 600 particles each have corresponding weights, we resample 450 particles using a uniform distribution with replacement. After we generate a new list of particles—many of which are exact duplicates—we create 450 new particles by adding uniform random noise. We found that a range of 1.2 meters by 1.2 meters and a heading range of 45 degrees are sufficient for allowing better guesses to be generated without spiking particle depletion of the best guesses. To ensure that we also avoid converging solely in the vicinity of our best guesses, we sample 30 random positions and corresponding headings with greater variance in heading to specifically avoid particle depletion of potentially accurate headings, assuming that the positions are already reasonably accurate.

**Notable Challenges**  
	We ran into many issues with RViz as well as SLAM. It took a long time to be able to properly use RViz to visualize the map, the particles, and the robot’s position. One of our issues was that whenever we moved the robot, the map would get distorted. This was because we didn’t initially follow the step of disabling SLAM before running the filter. Additionally, we had issues with the odom frame not being usable with the map frame. This was because in our code we had base\_frame set to base\_footprint instead of base\_link. Our odom frame was connected to the map frame via base\_link instead of base\_footprint, so we had to change base\_frame to base\_link.

**Important Lessons**  
	We learned that it is vital to test needed software early on with components of the larger project as we implement them—especially RViz. We also learned the value of testing iterative buildouts more than one week in advance of project deadlines, and that it is vital to read through installing all necessary dependencies and completing all required setup steps before testing any implementations.

**Future Improvements**  
	To further improve our particle filter, there are three main developments that are feasible to build out using our current particle filter. The first is to generate and resample particle clouds using a Gaussian distribution, ensuring that there is a more normal and theoretically accurate sampling of particles to use in the particle filter given an initial guess. The next would be to tune particle parameters quantitatively by running simulations of the particle filter for a set of strict Neato movements and scoring their accuracy using either gradient descent or specifying specific parameters to test. Finally, we could also implement functionality to account for robot kidnapping: the scenario where there is no initial guess. To implement this, we would expand our initial particle cloud to encompass the entire map and constantly include a significant number of random particles spanning the same area to avoid convergence onto deceptively good guesses.

**Running our Particle Filter**

1. Follow the steps outlined in the [computational setup](https://comprobo26.github.io/How%20to/setup_your_environment) ([https\://comprobo26.github.io/How%20to/setup\_your\_environment](https://comprobo26.github.io/How%20to/setup_your_environment))  
2. Install required dependencies via:  
   pip3 install scikit-learn && sudo apt install \-y ros-jazzy-nav2-map-server \\  
   	ros-jazzy-nav2-amcl \\  
   	ros-jazzy-slam-toolbox \\  
   	python3-pykdl  
3. Run the following commands in terminal:  
   1. ros2 launch neato2\_gazebo neato\_gauntlet\_world.py  
   2. ros2 launch slam\_toolbox online\_sync\_launch.py  
   3. rviz2 and use the settings from Particle\_filter.rviz  
   4. rviz2 \-d \~/ros2\_ws/src/Particle\_Estimation\_P2/robot\_localization/Particle\_filter.rviz  
4. Stop running slam (press ctrl+c) in the terminal where you ran slam  
5. Run ros2 launch particle\_estimation\_p2 test\_pf.py map\_yaml:=/home/user/ros2\_ws/src/particle\_estimation\_p2/maps/gauntlet.yaml  
6. Place initial pose in rviz2 and drive the neato using tele-op
